newsitem.title: JAPAN: Official Japan again on defensive over a crisis.
newsitem.headline: Official Japan again on defensive over a crisis.

text.p: Japan's bureaucracy is again being criticised over its handling of an emergency -- this time for responding too quickly.

The coastguard, sharply criticised for a slow response to an oil spill from a Russian tanker in January, raised the panic alarm on Wednesday by grossly over-estimating the size of a leak from a supertanker that hit a reef in Tokyo Bay.
The agency said the tanker had leaked an estimated 14,000 tonnes, which would make it the biggest oil spill in the history of Japan.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto reacted strongly, declaring the spill an emergency and mobilising a huge flotilla of ships to fight the spill and prevent what looked like an impending environmental disaster.
But embarrassed officials said on Thursday morning that the spill probably only totalled one-tenth that amount. The Exxon Valdez spill in Alaska released 25 times more oil.

"We apologise to citizens and to those who were directly affected for having raised grave concerns," Transport Minister Makoto Koga told a news conference. The Transport Ministry supervises the coastguard.
But the agency itself refused to offer an apology, saying only that they erred on the side of caution.
Hashimoto seemed unconcerned as well that the government may have misjudged the incident.
"It was a miracle... The oil had filled up an empty storage hold instead of spreading in the water," Hashimoto told reporters after being told of the error.
Hashimoto was among those who loudly complained about the slow response to the January incident when a Russian tanker broke in two in the Sea of Japan.
The heavy sludge fouled more than 450 km (285 miles) of coastline yet the cleanup largely consisted of volunteers using ladles and buckets.
That criticism followed strong debate over the handling of the 1995 Kobe earthquake. Two years after the massive quake, nearly 70,000 people were still living in temporary homes.
Japanese media said the government has still not learned its lessons.

"The Transport Ministry and others used calculations and information from the shipowner (of the tanker) without collating data with third parties," the daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun said in Thursday's evening edition.
"We do not consider this a mistake," said Shigehiro Sakamoto, chief of Security and Rescue at the Yokohama regional coastguard headquarters.
"It was better that we raised the alarm and we only erred on the side of caution. Anyway, we were able to get a full-scale disaster operation up and running quickly and that's what counts."
It was not the first time that officials have leapt before they looked.
Hashimoto declared a national emergency when an earthquake with an initially strong reading hit the southern island of Kyushu in April.
In the end, only one house was damaged and no one was injured.
